extracted.intended_audience: editors, proofreaders, compositors, and authors preparing manuscript typography and style
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for punctuation, hyphenation, word division, footnotes, indexing, tabular composition, and technical typographic conventions used in book and journal production. Intended to govern copyediting, typesetting, and proofreading decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation of self- compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Compound words in which the first element is 'self' are hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: self-evident, self-respect (see 119, note).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compounds with 'fold'
rubrics_metrics.description: Combinations with 'fold' are printed as one word if the number contains only one syllable; if it contains more, as two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: twofold, tenfold; fifteen fold, a hundred fold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjectives formed with suffix '-like'
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjectives formed by suffixation of 'like' to a noun are usually printed as one word if the noun contains only one syllable (except when ending in l); if the noun contains more syllables (or is a proper noun), they should be hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: childlike, homelike, warlike, godlike; eel-like, bell-like; woman-like, business-like; American-like (but: Christlike).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation in titles with parts such as Vice, ex-, elect, general, lieutenant
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Vice,' 'ex-,' 'elect,' 'general,' and 'lieutenant,' when constituting parts of titles, should be connected with the chief noun by a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Vice-Consul Taylor, ex-President Cleveland, the governor-elect, the postmaster-general, a lieutenant-colonel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compounds beginning with 'by-'
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'by-' when this word forms the first element of the compound should be hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: by-product, by-laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation of prefixes 'co-', 'pre-', 're-' (general rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The prefixes 'co-,' 'pre-,' and 're-,' when followed by the same vowel as that in which they terminate, or by w or y, take a hyphen; as a rule they do not when followed by a different vowel or by a consonant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: co-operation, pre-empted, re-enter, co-worker, re-yield; but: coequal, coceducation, prearranged, reinstal; cohabitation, prehistoric, recast (re-read).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation exceptions for re-/co-/pre-
rubrics_metrics.description: Exceptions include combinations with proper names, long or unusual formations, and words where omission would convey a different meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: pre-Raphaelite, re-tammanize; re-postpone, re-pulverization; re-formation (vs. reformation), re-cover (= cover again), re-creation. Note: some journals (e.g., Botanical Gazette) print cooperate, reenter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omitted hyphen in certain compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit the hyphen in a small list of established compounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: today, tomorrow, tonight, viewpoint, standpoint. (See 119g.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative particles un-, in-, a- (usual treatment)
rubrics_metrics.description: The negative particles 'un-,' 'in-,' and 'a-' do not usually require a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: unmanly, undemocratic, inanimate, indeterminate, illimitable, impersonal, asymmetrical. Exceptions are rare and artificial combinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefix 'non-' (usual treatment)
rubrics_metrics.description: The particle 'non-' ordinarily calls for a hyphen, except in the commonest words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples requiring hyphen: non-aesthetic, non-subservient, non-contagious, non-ability, non-interference, non-unionist, non-membership; but common words without hyphen: nonage, nondescript, nonessential, nonplus, nonsense, noncombatant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefix 'quasi-'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Quasi-' prefixed to a noun or an adjective requires a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: quasi-corporation, quasi-historical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefixes 'over-' and 'under-'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Over' and 'under' prefixed to a word should not be followed by a hyphen, except in unusual cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: overbold, overemphasize, overweight, underfed, underestimate, undersecretary; but: over-soul, under-man, over-spiritualistic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latin preposition prefixes (ante-, anti-, inter-, intra-, post-, sub-, super-)
rubrics_metrics.description: These prefixes do not ordinarily require a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: antedate, antechamber, antediluvian, antidote, antiseptic (but: anti-imperialistic—cf. 203), international, interstate, intercity, intramural (but: intra-atomic), postscript, postgraduate, postprandial, subconscious, submarine, subtitle, subway, superfine. Exceptions: ante-bellum, ante-Nicene, anti-Semitic, inter-university, post-revolutionary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefixes extra-, infra-, pan-, supra-, ultra-
rubrics_metrics.description: These prefixes, as a rule, call for a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: extra-hazardous, infra-mundane, pan-Hellenic, supra-temporal, ultra-conservative (but: Ultramontane).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation in fractional numbers (spelled out)
rubrics_metrics.description: In fractional numbers spelled out, connect the numerator and the denominator by a hyphen, unless either already contains a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'two-thirds', 'four and five-sevenths', 'thirty-hundredths'; but: 'thirty-one hundredths'. Do not hyphenate in constructions such as 'One half of his fortune...'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphen indicating omitted common element
rubrics_metrics.description: When two or more compound words occurring together have one component element in common, omit that element in all but the last word and indicate the omission by a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in English- and German-speaking countries; one-, five-, and ten-cent pieces; fifth- and tenth-century Europe. Note: some writers regard this hyphen as Teutonism (see note).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphen to indicate prefix/suffix as particle or incomplete syllable
rubrics_metrics.description: A hyphen is used to indicate a prefix or a suffix as a particle or syllable not complete in itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'The prefix a-'; 'The German diminutive suffixes -chen and -lezn.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphen to indicate syllabication
rubrics_metrics.description: A hyphen is employed to indicate the syllables of a word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: di-a-gram, pho-tog-ra-phy.

rubrics_metrics.name: List of common hyphenated everyday words
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain everyday compound words should be hyphenated even if not covered by earlier rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples listed: after-years, cross-section, man-of-war, son-in-law, bas-relief, death-rate, object-lesson, subject-matter, birth-rate, folk-song, page-proof, thought-process, blood-relations, food-stuff, pay-roll, title-page, coat-of-arms, fountain-head, poor-law, wave-length, common-sense, guinea-pig, post-office, well-being, cross-examine, horse-power, sea-level, well-nigh, cross-reference, loan-word, sense-perception, will-power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary word divisions (general rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid all unnecessary divisions of words. Wherever consistent with good spacing, carry the whole word over into the next line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize good spacing over forced divisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not divide on two-letter syllables in wide measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not, in wide measures (20 ems or more), divide on a syllable of two letters, if possible to avoid it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Never carry over a syllable of two letters. Words of four letters should never be divided; words of five or six rarely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit on lines terminating in hyphen
rubrics_metrics.description: Never let more than two consecutive lines terminate in a hyphen, if at all avoidable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The next-to-last line in a paragraph ought not to end in a divided word; the last line ('breakline') should, in measures of 15 ems and up, contain at least four letters. Avoid a divided word at the bottom of a right-hand (recto) page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not divide proper nouns or initials
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not divide proper nouns, especially names of persons, unless absolutely necessary. Do not separate initials of a name or combinations like A.D., P.M., etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carry such elements intact to the next line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid separation of divisional marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the separation of a divisional mark (e.g., (a) or (1)) in the middle of a sentence from the section which it precedes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not allow such mark to fall at the end of a line; carry it over with the matter to which it pertains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide according to pronunciation (American system)
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide words according to pronunciation (the American system), not according to derivation (the English system).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: democ-racy, not demo-cracy; knowledge: knowl-edge, not know-ledge. As far as compatible with pronunciation and good spacing, divide compounds on etymological lines or according to derivation and meaning (dis-pleasure preferred to displeas-ure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Division between consonants when syllable ends on one consonant
rubrics_metrics.description: When two consonants meet between vowels, and the syllable ends on one consonant, division may properly be made between the consonants, the pronunciation determining the place of division.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: advan-tage, exces-sive, finan-cier, foun-da-tion, impor-tant, In-dian, moun-tain, profes-sor, struc-ture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not terminate a line in soft 'c', 'g', or 'j'
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not terminate a line in a soft c or g, or in a j. Avoid the division entirely if possible; if not, divide so the soft sound is carried appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferred: pro-cess (not proc-ess); ne-cessary (not nec-essary); spacing: pro-geny not prog-eny; pre-judice not prej-udice. Note: this differs from some dictionary rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide on a vowel where practicable; exceptions for -able/-ible
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide on a vowel wherever practicable. Exception: words in -able and -ible should carry the vowel over into the next line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: sepa-rate (not sep-arate); particu-lar (not partic-ular); read-able (not reada-ble); convert-ible (not converti-ble).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid additional hyphens within hyphenated nouns/adjectives
rubrics_metrics.description: In hyphenated nouns and adjectives, avoid creating additional hyphens by dividing within elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: object-lesson (not object-les-son); fellow-being (not fel-low-being); poverty-stricken (not pover-ty-stricken).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat diphthongs as single letters for division
rubrics_metrics.description: A coalition of two vowel-sounds into one (a diphthong) should be treated as one letter; do not divide within it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not divide: peo-ple (either syllable makes a bad division), Cae-sar, bu-ilding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division rules for derivatives with shifted accent
rubrics_metrics.description: In derivatives from words ending in a letter whose accent has shifted, the letter in divisions should be carried into the next line with the suffix if the accent has been shifted; if the derivative retains the accent of the parent-word, the letter should be left in the first line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: objec-tive (from ob'ject); defect-ive (from defect'); but: respec-tively, distinc-tive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not divide added plural 's' syllables
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding a plural s that creates an additional syllable in words ending in an s-sound does not justify dividing such words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'hor-ses' and 'circumstan-ces' are impossible divisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of adjectives in -ical
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjectives ending in -ical should be divided on the 'i' of -ical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: physi-cal (not phys-ical nor physic-al).

rubrics_metrics.name: Condensed language-specific division rules — French
rubrics_metrics.description: Fundamental principle: divide on a vowel as far as possible, avoiding consonantal ending of syllables. Two consonants where second is l or r (but not certain combos) are both carried over; there are as many syllables as vowels even if soundless; mute 'e' following a vowel does not form a syllable; certain letters when preceding vowels may be sounded as consonants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in-di-vi-si-bi-li-té, a-che-ter; ta-bleau (not tab-leau); bien, é-tions, yeux.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condensed language-specific division rules — German
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide on a vowel as far as possible. If several consonants stand between vowels, usually only the last is carried over. Certain combinations (sz, ch, sch, ph, st, th) are never separated. If ck must be divided, separate k-k. In foreign words, consonant combinations with z or r are carried over. Compound words are separated first into components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: hii-ten, le-ben, Fa-brik; Rit-ter, klir-ren; Bu-sze, Geo-gra-phie; Deckel—Dek-kel; Fiirsten-schlosz, Tiir-an-gel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condensed language-specific division rules — Italian
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide on a vowel as far as possible. Do not separate s before a consonant, certain digraphs (ch, gh, gli, gn, qu, sc, etc.) are never separated. i=y and u=w go with following vowel; some vowel groups are not separated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ta-vo-lf-no, nar-ra-re; ca-st{-ghi, a-vro, mi-gli6-re; miéi, tudi.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condensed language-specific division rules — Spanish
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide on a vowel as far as possible. Treat ch, ll, rr as simple consonants; cc and mn are divided as in English. Liquid consonants l and r when preceded by consonant (other than s) must not be separated from that consonant except in compounds; two separable consonants should be divided; s is always disjoined from a following consonant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ca-ra-co-les, mu-cha-cho, ba-ta-lla, bu-ll6, ci-ga-rro; ac-ce-so, en-no-ble-cer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condensed language-specific division rules — Greek
rubrics_metrics.description: Single consonants, consonant combinations that can begin a word, and mutes followed by 'u' or 'y' are placed at beginning of a syllable; other consonant combinations are divided. Compound words are divided into original parts, then rules apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: é&-xw, é-yo, pu-Kpdv, mwpoo-d-yw.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condensed language-specific division rules — Latin
rubrics_metrics.description: A Latin word has as many syllables as vowels/diphthongs. When a single consonant occurs between two vowels, divide before the consonant. For two or more consonants, divide before the last consonant except certain mute+liquid combinations and gu/gu.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Cae-sar, me-ri-di-es; om-nis, scrip-tus; ad-est, ab-rum-po.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use superior figures for footnote reference indices (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: For reference indices, as a rule, use superior figures. Only in special cases should asterisks, daggers, etc., be used (e.g., tabular or algebraic matter). Index figures in the text should be placed after the punctuation marks, without space, except in German where they are placed inside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When figures are not used, use sequence: * (asterisk), † (dagger), ‡ (double dagger), § (section mark), || (parallels), ¶ (paragraph mark). Place index figure at end of quotation as a rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ibid., loc. cit., op. cit.
rubrics_metrics.description: Where references to the same work follow each other closely and uninterruptedly, use ibid. instead of repeating the title. Ibid. takes the place of as much of the previous reference as is repeated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ibid. should not ordinarily be used for the first footnote on a verso (left-hand) page; better to repeat the title if short or use loc. cit. (when reference is to entire citation) or op. cit. (when work only is cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Footnotes to tables formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Footnotes to tables, whether the tables are ruled or open, should be set in 6-pt and placed at the foot of the table (not the foot of the page). For reference indices in such cases use asterisks, etc., not superior figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See 234. Use consistent sizing and placement to avoid confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit author's name in footnote when given in text
rubrics_metrics.description: If the author's name is given in the text in connection with a reference to, or a quotation from, his work, it should not be repeated in the footnote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place index figure in the text at the end of the quotation (preferred).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviations in references (Vol., chap., p.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinarily omit 'Vol.,' 'chap.,' and 'p.' in references to particular passages. Use Roman numerals (capitals) for Volume, Book, Part, and Division except in references to ancient/classical authors where lower-case roman numerals should be used; Arabic numerals for number and text pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only use 'Vol., p.' etc. when confusion would arise or in exceptional cases; where reference is to a page alone, the abbreviation 'p.' or 'pp.' must be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Footnote numbering for linotype composition
rubrics_metrics.description: In work set on the linotype machine, footnotes should be numbered consecutively through an article (in a journal) or through a chapter (in a book) to save resetting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions noted for specific journals (e.g., Botanical Gazette numbers footnotes consecutively through an article; many journals number from 1 on each page).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: treatment of Mac/Mc/M', St., Ste.
rubrics_metrics.description: Names beginning with Mac, Mc, or M', St., Ste., whether following letter is capitalized or not, should be listed as if the prefix were spelled Mac, Saint, Sainte to prevent the user searching several places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: MacIntyre, Henry; M’Intyre, Thomas; St. Louis; Sainte Beuve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: compound names listed under first part
rubrics_metrics.description: Compound names should be listed under the first part of the name. List the other parts of the names in their respective alphabetical positions and give a cross-reference to the first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Campbell-Bannerman, Sir Henry; Lloyd-George, David; provide cross-reference: George, Lloyd-, David. See Lloyd-George.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: names with prefixes (general treatment and exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Names with prefixes should be listed under the part following the prefix, except: (i) in English (see compound-name rule), (ii) in French when prefix contains the article, (iii) in Italian/Spanish when prefix is simply the article, (iv) in Dutch where Van/Ten etc. are always capitalized, (v) when prefix and name are written as one word. Naturalized names with prefixes should be treated according to the language adopted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Hoffman, von; Lima, de; Ponte e Horto, da; Santos Pereira Jardin, dos. English examples: A Becket; De Quincey; De Morgan; D’Israeli; MacDonald; Van Buren.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: umlaut and diacritic spelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Names spelled with the umlaut (ä, ö, ü) should be listed as if the umlaut were spelled out (ae, oe, ue).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Müller listed as Mueller; Miiller, A.; Muller, B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: names connected by 'and', '&', 'y', 'et', 'und', 'e'
rubrics_metrics.description: Names or firms connected by conjunctions or equivalents should be listed according to the first letter of the name preceding the connective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Smith & Evans (under 'S'); Gomez y Pineda (under 'G'); Loubet et Meunier (under 'L'); Duncker und Humblot (under 'D'); Sandrone e Vallardi (under 'S').

rubrics_metrics.name: Tabular type size rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidelines for type sizes used in tables depending on body matter size and whether tables are open (unruled) or ruled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: In 11-pt. and 10-pt. matter open tables ordinarily set in 9-pt. leaded; ruled tables in 8-pt. solid. In 9-pt. matter both open and ruled tables set in 8-pt. solid. In 8-pt. matter open in 6-pt. leaded; ruled in 6-pt. solid. In 6-pt. matter both open and ruled in 6-pt. solid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table typography: column captions and box-heads
rubrics_metrics.description: Captions for columns of open tables and box-heads for ruled tables should ordinarily be set in 6-pt. For multi-story box-heads, set upper (primary) heads in caps and small caps, lower (secondary) in caps and lower case. Where small caps used in box-heads, the 'stub' head should also be in caps and small caps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If second story consists only of figures, follow different conventions (see p.92).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing between table rules and matter
rubrics_metrics.description: In ruled tables there should be at least two leads space between the horizontal rules and the matter inclosed, and if practicable at least the equivalent of an en quad of the type between the perpendicular rules and the matter inclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain clear breathing space between rules and content for legibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaders and separators in tables
rubrics_metrics.description: In open tables either periods (one em apart and aligned) or leaders may be used between columns. In ruled tables, in the stub, leaders should usually be employed if there is room.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A leader is type with dots or short lines used to lead the eye across to the right word or number.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment and spacing of figures in table columns
rubrics_metrics.description: In columns of figures, to express a blank use leaders across full width. Center figures in the column; if exact centering impossible due to unequal digit groups, leave more space on the left than on the right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When there is reading-matter in columns of a ruled table, center if possible; if any line runs over, use hanging indention and align all on the left.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table rule conventions (double rules and vertical rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Double rules should be used at the top of all tables. Vertical (perpendicular) rules used usually only when a table is doubled up on itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tables of two columns only should be set as open; three or more as ruled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table headline formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Table I,' etc., in headlines of tables should ordinarily be set in caps of the type in which the body of the table is set; the following descriptive line, if any, in caps and small caps of same type. A single descriptive headline not preceded by number should be set in caps of the table body type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow specimen examples for consistent table titling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point system and pica as standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The point is the underlying unit of all typographical measures. The standard of measurement is the pica; a pica is twelve points (one-sixth of an inch).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common type sizes and names enumerated: 12-pt (pica), 11-pt (small pica), 10-pt (long primer), 9-pt (bourgeois), 8-pt (brevier), 7-pt (minion), 6-pt (nonpareil), 5-pt (pearl?). Sizes larger or smaller seldom used in book composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Styles of type (roman, italic, boldface) and notation in manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinary type called roman; italics indicated in manuscript by a straight line under the word(s); bold face indicated by a wavy line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples shown in manual for identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typographic anatomy (shank, face, kern, shoulder, cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions of parts of type: body (shank), face (bearing the character), kern (face projecting beyond shank), shoulder (shank projecting beyond face). A font includes caps, small caps, and lower-case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manuscript notation for caps (three straight lines), small caps (two), etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotype vs. linotype spacing systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Monotype uses a unit system: standard spaces are fixed unit spaces (6-unit, 5-unit, 4-unit). Linotype uses the pica system with fixed em/en/thin spaces and space bands to spread spaces between specified ranges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monotype: standard space = 6-unit (3-em) etc. Linotype: fixed spaces (em quad, en quad, thin) and space bands for justification; very thin spaces must be inserted by hand if smaller than thin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and use of em, en, and other spaces/dashes
rubrics_metrics.description: An em (em quad) is a square block (unit of measurement); an en quad is half an em. Three-em (thick space) is standard space between words. Jour-em and five-em spaces, hair-spaces defined. Em/en/3-em/2-em dashes defined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and demonstration lines provided for each space/dash type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing after punctuation (standard line spacing rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard line should have a 3-em space between words not separated by punctuation other than commas, and after commas; an en quad after semicolons and colons followed by a lower-case letter; two 3-em spaces after colons followed by a capital; an em quad after periods, exclamation, and interrogation points concluding a sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow this spacing hierarchy to achieve even typographic color.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjusting spacing when justifying lines
rubrics_metrics.description: If necessary to reduce spacing in a line, begin with commas and letters of slanting form; if increasing, begin with overlapping letters and points other than periods and commas, in this order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this order to choose which spaces/letters to alter when justifying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion guideline for well-spaced lines
rubrics_metrics.description: In a well-spaced line with a 3-em space between a majority of words, there should not be more than an en quad between the rest; maintain this proportion when increasing or reducing spacing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid following very thin-spaced lines with very wide-spaced lines; never hair-space or em-quad a line to avoid a run-over; do not space out last line of paragraph leaving an em or more indention at the end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing around short words and symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Short words like 'a,' 'an,' etc., should have the same space on each side. Use a thin space after §, ¶, and similar signs; before 'f.' 'ff.' and metric symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In American/English sums of money no space used between currency symbol ($, £) and numerals; an en leader used for decimal point in examples given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing after numerals in headings and small-cap usage
rubrics_metrics.description: After Arabic and Roman numerals at the beginning of subsections, use an en quad. After such numerals at the beginning of center-heads use an em quad. Small-cap headings should have an en quad between words; cap-and-small-cap and cap headings two 3-em spaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply consistent spacing for hierarchical headings.

rubrics_metrics.name: No space between letters forming products and before superior/inferior figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Between letters forming products, and before superior figures or letters indicating powers, and inferior figures or letters, ordinarily no space should be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given in mathematical expressions; adhere to typographic compactness for formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indentation rules by measure width and type size
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific indentation amounts depend on measure width and type size: e.g., measures under 10 picas indent 1 em; measures 10–20 picas indent vary by type size; measures 20–30 picas have larger indents. Hanging indention values differ by range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table-like guidelines given: apply specified em values for plain paragraphs and hanging indentions according to type size and measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indentation and alignment rules for poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: In poetry, center the longest line and let indentation be governed by that; if longest line is disproportionately long, use an average of long lines. When consecutive quoted poems vary slightly in line length, indent all alike. Indent according to rhymes and length of lines; align blank verse and consecutive rhyming lines as described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If rhymes alternate, indent rhyming lines alike (usually one em). If any line is disproportionately short, indent it more. Several illustrative examples provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for plain paragraphs and use of hanging indention
rubrics_metrics.description: In ordinary reading-matter 'plain paragraphs' are preferable. Use 'hanging indention' when it is desired to bring into relief the opening word(s) of a paragraph, or where a center-head makes more than three lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply hanging indention selectively for emphasis or layout necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leads and slugs definitions and usage
rubrics_metrics.description: A lead is a strip of metal used to separate lines of type; ordinary lead is 2 points thick. A slug is a thicker strip of metal used in make-up, standard sizes 6 and 12 points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between leaded (with leads between lines) and solid (without) setting in book composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting center-heads and multi-line headings
rubrics_metrics.description: A center-head is a headline placed equidistant from both margins, usually set in caps or small caps. When center-head makes more than one line, use inverted 'pyramid' form for two/three lines or 'hanging indention' for more than three lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided; use pyramid for shorter multi-line headlines and hanging indentation for longer ones.
